summary.qualitative: The candidate is strongest in section E and in the pivot design (exchanges, session-level pass, $0.002/session, cold-read target), where it matches the reference closely and stays grounded. It is much weaker in section A, omitting nearly all tool-level friction the reference captures (zsh `======`, transcript-parser rewrite, spine_entries patch and rubric sizing, Keychain/config-dir deviation, the chosen linux-ssh topic, the arm-B bar), and it never names the repo path. Section C is its biggest liability: several user attributions are invented or reversed (user 'cited' the repos convention, 'did mental math', 'invoked live data is sacred', 'understood TypeSafe immediately', 'accepted via follow-up' when no follow-up exists), and D introduces non-spec origins ('Pragmatism', 'Principle') and a fabricated security rationale. Net: decent structure and outcome fidelity, but recall of granular evidence is low and grounding in the user-model sections is unreliable.

candidate_claims.note: Failures are real; omits that the Python passes also yielded nothing useful (five attempts total).
Called 'Bash wrapper'; it is a zsh function — trivial.
No such friction; api.md/choice.md/python.md and models.md were fetched directly.
candidate_claims.reason: No iteration or friction on TypeSafe API call format occurred anywhere; api.md, choice.md, python.md and models.md were curled directly and succeeded first time. The asserted iteration episode has no referent to distort.

candidate_claims.note: The user framed it as a bug; the assistant never assumed so.
candidate_claims.reason: The 'bug' framing genuinely exists in the transcript — it is the user's — and the claim reassigns it to the assistant. Wrong actor on a real framing.

candidate_claims.note: Binary only said <quote withheld>.
candidate_claims.reason: The binary's security rationale for never saving home trust is real; 'prevents privilege escalation in shared environments' embellishes an unstated specific onto it. Over-claimed detail.
The assistant never held or expressed any assumption of even cost distribution; it measured the transcripts and reported ~90% tool I/O. Invented assumption.

candidate_claims.note: Table showed three sessions; ranges extrapolated but consistent.
Assistant addressed cross-turn signals directly in its first reply on the pivot.
candidate_claims.reason: Cross-turn/multi-block signals were addressed directly in the assistant's first reply on the pivot; the claim reverses the direction of a real event.

candidate_claims.note: Session ends on the assistant's turn; no user follow-up exists.
candidate_claims.reason: The session ends on the assistant's turn; no user follow-up exists to signal acceptance. Invented event.

candidate_claims.note: User explicitly said <quote withheld>; ledger existence is recorded knowledge (since v1.1.13).
candidate_claims.reason: The PC ground-truth/ledger topic is real, but the claim reverses the state: the user explicitly offered to copy sessions and the ledger is recorded knowledge. Wrong direction.

candidate_claims.note: $0.042/Mtok and $0.002/session grounded; '~2k tokens per session' is invented and inconsistent with the price math.
candidate_claims.reason: The pricing arithmetic ($0.042/Mtok, ~$0.002/session) is grounded; the '~2k tokens per session' figure is a wrong number inside the real calculation.

candidate_claims.note: No user response after the pricing calculation.
candidate_claims.reason: The pricing calculation is the assistant's final turn; no user response follows. The acceptance and shift of focus are invented events.

candidate_claims.note: Convention came from the knowledge base; user never cited it.
candidate_claims.reason: The <user-repos-root><project> convention is real in the transcript but came from the knowledge base file, not from the user citing it. Wrong actor.

candidate_claims.note: User asked for an executive summary of what the skill does.
candidate_claims.reason: Same shape as other expertise claims: the user's real request for an explanation of the skill is inverted into immediate understanding of System One models. Over-claimed/reversed.

candidate_claims.note: User never commented on it.
candidate_claims.reason: The user never responded to or acknowledged the trust findings at all. An acceptance/non-surprise reaction is invented, with no reaction in the transcript to be a distortion of.

candidate_claims.note: All done by the assistant.
candidate_claims.reason: The doc reading, Mtok/Btok pricing comprehension and $0.002/session math all really happened — performed by the assistant, not the user. Wrong actor.

candidate_claims.note: pkill/systemd came from the assistant's synthetic query; only KB-supported, not demonstrated.
candidate_claims.reason: These topics really appear (PortCall hooks, MCP stripping, headless cells, and pkill/systemd in the assistant's synthetic query), but the claim over-attributes them as user-demonstrated expertise.

candidate_claims.note: Assistant's assumption, misattributed as a user growth edge.
candidate_claims.reason: The uncertainty about the answers.file.choice field name is real — it is the assistant's flagged assumption, misattributed to the user. Wrong actor.

candidate_claims.note: Assistant's proposal / KB open question, not a user statement.
candidate_claims.reason: The cold-read vs warm recall validation is real in the transcript, but it is the assistant's proposal/KB open question, not a user-stated want. Wrong actor.

Both the principle ('live data is sacred', surfaced from the knowledge base) and the PC ground-truth collection are real in the transcript; the claim wrongly attributes the invocation to the user as explicit justification. Wrong actor/attribution.

candidate_claims.note: It was item 2 of 3.
candidate_claims.reason: The trust item is really in the user's request, but as item 2 of 3, not first. Wrong ordering detail.

candidate_claims.note: Only one replacement cell ran at $1.00; cells 2–3 ran under $0.50.
candidate_claims.reason: A real $1.00-cap replacement cell ran; the claim inflates it to 3 cells completing under that cap. Wrong number.

candidate_claims.note: Never invoked; the basis was the recorded 'marks' case plus measured token arithmetic.
candidate_claims.reason: The 'live data is sacred' principle exists in the transcript (KB core value) and the pivot is real; the claim mis-states the pivot's cause, which was the recorded 'marks' case plus token arithmetic. Wrong cause.

candidate_claims.note: Assistant's stated reason: different question, both small; and it was a proposal pending user OK, not a decision.
candidate_claims.reason: The separate-repo proposal and the repos-under-parent-folder convention both exist; the claim mis-states the rationale (different question, both small) and treats a pending proposal as a decision. Wrong cause.

candidate_claims.note: 4 cells, 3 valid (cell 1 budget-exhausted).
candidate_claims.reason: 4 cells ran but only 3 were valid (cell 1 was budget-exhausted). Wrong number.

candidate_claims.note: Transcript has 9 turns; ~40 min unverifiable; rest grounded.
candidate_claims.reason: Real session statistics with a wrong count (9 turns, not 8) and an unverifiable duration; the rest (commits, repo, tool count) is grounded.

candidate_claims.note: Privilege escalation/sandboxing never discussed.
candidate_claims.reason: Privilege escalation, sandboxing and distributed systems are not discussed anywhere in the session; these domains are invented rather than mis-stated versions of real topics.

candidate_claims.note: User has not approved; assistant asked for repo-split decision.
candidate_claims.reason: project.py as a pending, not-yet-written step is real; the claim mis-states its status as 'design approved' when the assistant was still awaiting the user's repo-split decision. Over-claimed status of a real item.

candidate_claims.note: No count given; Jev is not trained.
candidate_claims.reason: The PC session copy is a real, user-proposed plan; the '~50+ sessions' count is invented and 'training' mischaracterizes Jev's use. Wrong number/characterization on a real referent.
